title: Managing stakeholder expectations
blurb: Explain why a project that hits every target can still be judged a failure, and how to keep expectations realistic from start to handover.
question: A new HR system goes live on time, within budget and meeting every agreed requirement. Yet the department heads say the project has failed, because they expected it to automate holiday booking too. Why has this happened, and what should the project manager have done?

teach.h: Expectations: what stakeholders believe they will get
teach.body: Expectations are what stakeholders believe the project will deliver, when, at what cost and to what standard. Managing expectations means understanding them, shaping them and agreeing them so that they match what the project can realistically deliver, then keeping them aligned as things change. In plain English: no nasty surprises. Everyone should know what they are getting, what they are not getting, and why.

teach.h: Why it is critical to success
teach.body: Stakeholders judge success against what they expected, not against the project's internal targets. If expectations are left unmanaged, stakeholders can be dissatisfied even when the project meets its time, cost and quality targets. Unrealistic expectations also drive late requests, disputes over scope, conflict between stakeholders, loss of trust in the project manager and resistance to using the outputs, which puts the benefits at risk.

teach.caption: The aim is to grow the overlap: make expectations explicit and agree them, so what is expected is what is delivered.

teach.body: Members hoped the pool would reopen for the summer holidays. The project manager showed the realistic schedule early: reopening in September. Swimming clubs helped choose between a shorter closure with fewer changing rooms or the full refit (involved in decisions). Acceptance criteria for water temperature and accessibility were agreed with the operator. When a pump delivery slipped two weeks, members heard within a day, with the new date and the reason. Reopening was praised, even though it was autumn.

teach.caption: In iterative work, stakeholders must understand from the start that scope flexes: Could have items may not make it.

teach.text: Exam trap: when a stakeholder is unhappy although every target was met, the answer is misaligned expectations, not poor performance. And managing expectations is NOT promising stakeholders what they want to hear: over-promising widens the gap you will have to close later.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Say why it matters: success is judged against expectations, not just targets.
Give a consequence: dissatisfaction, disputes, scope creep or lost support.
Agree realistic scope, time, cost and acceptance criteria early.
Be honest about constraints and report progress and issues early.
Involve stakeholders in decisions and changes so expectations stay aligned.
Unmanaged expectations cause dissatisfaction even when targets are met.
Agree realistic scope, time and cost, and confirm acceptance criteria.
Be honest about constraints and change; report progress and issues early.
Involve stakeholders in decisions, especially trade-offs.
Iterative projects must set the expectation that scope flexes (MoSCoW).

summary: You can now explain why managing stakeholder expectations is critical to project success, including why a project can hit its targets and still be seen as a failure. You can also describe the practical ways to set and keep expectations realistic in linear and iterative projects.

A.q: A website relaunch is delivered on time, on budget and to its agreed specification, but the marketing director calls it a disappointment. What is the most likely cause?
options: The budget was set too generously
The schedule was far too ambitious
Expectations were never aligned
The specification lacked any detail
A.why: If the agreed targets were all met but the stakeholder is still disappointed, their expectations differed from what was agreed: expectations were not managed.

whyNot.0: A generous budget does not explain disappointment with an output that met its specification.
whyNot.1: The schedule was met, so it was not too ambitious in practice.
whyNot.3: The specification was met; the gap is between it and what the director expected.

A.q: Which action does MOST to make sure stakeholders and the project agree on what a finished deliverable must achieve?
options: Agreeing acceptance criteria
Issuing a longer monthly report
Adding contingency to the budget
Asking the team to work overtime
A.why: Acceptance criteria set out, in advance, the measurable conditions a deliverable must meet, so 'done' means the same thing to everyone.

whyNot.1: A longer report doesn't create agreement on what 'done' means.
whyNot.2: Contingency handles cost risk; it doesn't define what is acceptable.
whyNot.3: Overtime may speed work up but does nothing to align expectations.

A.q: A project manager realises a key milestone will slip by three weeks. Why should stakeholders be told straight away rather than at the next quarterly review?
options: Quarterly reviews cannot cover delays
It lets them adjust and keeps trust
It moves the blame to the supplier
Early notice cancels out the delay
A.why: Early, honest news lets stakeholders plan around the change and protects trust; late surprises damage relationships and confidence in the project.

whyNot.0: Reviews can cover delays; the problem is waiting too long.
whyNot.2: Managing expectations is about honesty, not shifting blame.
whyNot.3: Telling people early doesn't remove the delay, it reduces its impact.

B.q: Which of the following is NOT a good way to manage stakeholder expectations?
options: Being honest about project constraints
Involving stakeholders in trade-offs
Reporting issues as soon as they arise
Saying yes to every new request
B.why: Agreeing to every request creates expectations the project cannot meet, leading to scope creep, overruns and greater disappointment later.

whyNot.0: Honesty about constraints keeps expectations realistic.
whyNot.1: Involvement in trade-offs builds understanding and ownership of decisions.
whyNot.2: Early reporting avoids surprises and protects trust.

B.q: Midway through building a new warehouse, the operations director asks for an extra loading bay 'as it was always assumed'. It is not in the agreed scope. What should the project manager do?
options: Add the bay to avoid upsetting him
Refuse and end the discussion there
Confirm the scope and raise a change
Ask the contractor to fit it quietly
B.why: Restating the agreed scope realigns expectations, and a formal change request lets the impact on time, cost and benefits be assessed and decided properly.

whyNot.0: Adding unagreed scope causes scope creep and builds unrealistic expectations.
whyNot.1: A flat refusal damages the relationship; the request may be valid as a change.
whyNot.3: Hidden work bypasses change control and is a serious governance failure.

B.q: On an iterative project, users expect every feature on the wish list in the first release. How should the project manager manage this?
options: Explain MoSCoW: low priorities may drop
Promise all features to keep users motivated
Extend the time box until every feature fits
Hide the backlog from users until go-live
B.why: In iterative work time and cost are fixed per time box and scope flexes, so users must understand MoSCoW priorities: Must haves come first and Could haves may be dropped.

whyNot.1: Promising everything sets up disappointment when scope flexes.
whyNot.2: Time boxes are fixed; scope flexes, not the deadline.
whyNot.3: Hiding the backlog destroys transparency and trust.

C.q: Which THREE actions help manage stakeholder expectations? 1. Confirm acceptance criteria  2. Hold back bad news until it is solved  3. Involve stakeholders in key decisions  4. Report progress and issues early
options: 1, 2 and 3
1, 2 and 4
2, 3 and 4
1, 3 and 4
C.why: Confirming acceptance criteria, involving stakeholders in decisions and reporting early all keep expectations realistic. Holding back bad news creates late surprises.

whyNot.0: Holding back bad news (2) damages trust and expectations.
whyNot.1: Holding back bad news (2) damages trust and expectations.
whyNot.2: Holding back bad news (2) is poor practice, and acceptance criteria (1) are missing.

C.q: Which statement BEST explains why managing expectations is critical to project success?
options: Expectations decide the project's budget
Stakeholders judge success by them
It removes the need for change control
It guarantees the project finishes early
C.why: Stakeholders judge the project against what they expected, so unmanaged expectations can turn a project that met its targets into a perceived failure.

whyNot.0: The budget comes from estimates and approval, not expectations.
whyNot.2: Change control is still needed; expectation management works alongside it.
whyNot.3: Managing expectations does not change the schedule itself.

C.q: A sponsor announces to the board that a new CRM system will be live in three months. The project manager's estimate says six. What is the best action?
options: Plan for three months and hope it works
Say nothing and report slippage later
Show the sponsor the evidence and agree
Cut testing quietly to meet three months
C.why: The project manager should share the evidence-based estimate with the sponsor promptly, explain the constraints and options, and agree a realistic baseline before expectations harden.

whyNot.0: Planning on hope locks in an expectation that will not be met.
whyNot.1: Staying silent turns a fixable mismatch into a late, trust-damaging surprise.
whyNot.3: Quietly cutting testing risks quality and is dishonest.

reteach.title: The kitchen refit that went 'wrong'
reteach.question: A builder fits a kitchen exactly to the drawing, on time and on budget. The owner is furious. How can that happen?

blocks.h: Built to the drawing, not to the dream
blocks.body: The owner had pictured a kitchen like the showroom: an island, soft-close drawers, under-cupboard lights. The drawing included none of these, but nobody walked through it with her or said what was left out. The builder hit every target and still lost a customer. A ten-minute conversation at the start, a clear list of what's in and out, and a call when the worktop was delayed would have changed everything.

rows.label: At the start
values: Walks through what's in and out

rows.label: When delayed
values: Owner finds out on the day
Rings that week with a new date

blocks.text: Builder A delivered exactly what was agreed. The problem was never the kitchen: it was the unmanaged expectation.

explain.body: Stakeholders measure success against what they expected. Unmanaged expectations lead to dissatisfaction even when targets are met, plus disputes, late requests and resistance to using the outputs.

test.q: What is the main risk of leaving stakeholder expectations unmanaged?
options: Stakeholders may be unhappy despite success
The project team may stop doing timesheets
The risk register may grow too long to read
The sponsor may ask for fewer status reports
test.why: Stakeholders judge against their expectations, so unmanaged expectations can make a project that met its targets look like a failure.

whyNot.2: Risk register length is not the main concern here.
whyNot.3: Report frequency is not the key consequence.

explain.body: Agree scope, time and cost based on sound estimates, not hopes. State exclusions clearly. Confirm acceptance criteria so everyone knows in advance what 'done' and 'good enough' mean.

test.q: Why should exclusions be written into the agreed scope?
options: To shorten the project schedule
To stop false assumptions of extras
To reduce the size of the project team
To avoid the need for acceptance tests
test.why: Stating what is out of scope prevents stakeholders assuming extras are included, which is a common source of misaligned expectations.

whyNot.0: Exclusions clarify scope; they don't shorten the schedule.
whyNot.2: Team size isn't the purpose of stating exclusions.

explain.body: Be open about constraints and what cannot be done. Report progress, issues and forecast changes as soon as they are known, with options. Bad news shared early is a problem; bad news found late is a breach of trust.

test.q: A supplier warns of a four-week delay. When should the project manager tell the affected stakeholders?
options: Only once the delay is certain
Only if the sponsor asks directly
At the next scheduled phase review
Promptly, with impact and options
test.why: Prompt, honest reporting with the likely impact and options keeps expectations realistic and lets stakeholders plan.

whyNot.0: Waiting for certainty can remove the chance to respond.
whyNot.1: Stakeholders shouldn't have to ask to learn of a significant delay.
whyNot.2: Waiting for a scheduled review lets the surprise grow.

explain.body: When trade-offs or changes arise, involve the affected stakeholders in deciding. People accept outcomes they helped choose. In iterative work this happens every time box, as the product owner and users reprioritise.

test.q: Why does involving stakeholders in trade-off decisions help manage their expectations?
options: It transfers decision risk to them
It means the sponsor need not decide
They accept what they helped choose
It removes the need to record changes
test.why: When stakeholders take part in a decision they understand its reasons and are far more likely to accept the result.

whyNot.0: Involvement is about understanding and ownership, not shifting risk.
whyNot.1: Governance roles still apply; the sponsor may still decide.
whyNot.3: Changes must still be recorded under change control.
